summary: Vatican City is a city-state located within the city of Rome, the smallest sovereign state in the world, and the center of the Roman Catholic Church and the residence of the Pope.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: The site of the Vatican is traditionally held to be where the Apostle Peter was martyred and buried; in the 4th century Emperor Constantine the Great built the old St. Peter's Basilica here, and from then on the popes established their authority in Rome. From 756 the popes ruled the Papal States in central Italy, and after the Kingdom of Italy captured Rome in 1870 the pope called himself the "Prisoner in the Vatican," until the 1929 Lateran Treaty established Vatican City State. The residents of this state are almost entirely clergy, Swiss Guards and Holy See personnel, and the state itself is the nerve center of the Catholic Church, so Catholics make up 100 percent.

religion.background: Vatican City State is the center of the worldwide Catholic Church, and the pope is both head of state and spiritual leader of Catholics around the world. The Papal States ruled central Italy for more than a thousand years; after their annexation by the Kingdom of Italy in 1870, the pope and the Italian government were at odds for half a century. In 1929 Pope Pius XI signed the Lateran Treaty with Mussolini's government, establishing Vatican City State with an area of only about 0.44 square kilometers. Today the residents of the Vatican are mainly clergy and staff, and citizenship depends on one's office rather than being acquired by birth.

language.official: The official language of Vatican City State is Italian; the official language of the Holy See is Latin.

ranking.name: Italian
ranking.description: The Vatican is completely surrounded by the city of Rome, and since the state was established by the 1929 Lateran Treaty, its administration, law and everyday affairs have been conducted in Italian. The Holy See's official newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano, is published in Italian, and most lay staff working in the Vatican are also Italian, so Italian is the main everyday language.

ranking.name: German
ranking.description: The status of German comes mainly from the Swiss Guard: since Pope Julius II recruited Swiss mercenaries in 1506, the guard has been responsible for protecting the pope; its members mostly come from German-speaking Switzerland, and the language of command is also German. In addition, there are many clergy from Germany and Austria in the Holy See, making German the second most commonly used language in the Vatican.

language.history: Latin has been the language of the Western church since ancient Roman times and remains the official language of the Holy See's formal documents, papal encyclicals and laws. The Second Vatican Council of 1962-1965 allowed Mass to be celebrated in local languages, and Latin's place in everyday liturgy declined accordingly. The administrative language of Vatican City State is Italian, the Swiss Guard uses German, and because the departments of the Holy See serve the church worldwide, English, French and Spanish are also used extensively.

ranking.name: Spaghetti alla carbonara
ranking.description: Pasta is tossed with a sauce made of egg yolks, Pecorino cheese and black pepper, then combined with pan-fried cured pork cheek (guanciale), giving a smooth, rich texture.
ranking.history: Carbonara is the representative dish of Roman cuisine, but its earliest written record appears only in the mid-20th century after the Second World War, so it is relatively young. One widely circulated account is that after the Allies liberated Rome in 1944, bacon and powdered eggs from American rations inspired local cooks; the name "carbonara" means "charcoal burner," and some also believe it is linked with the charcoal burners of the Apennine mountains, but neither explanation is conclusive. The Vatican itself has no independent culinary tradition, and what Holy See staff eat every day is this kind of Roman home cooking.

ranking.name: Cacio e pepe
ranking.description: Pasta is tossed with plenty of grated Pecorino Romano and freshly ground black pepper, with the starchy pasta water emulsifying it into a creamy sauce; there are only three main ingredients.
ranking.history: "Cacio e pepe" means "cheese and pepper" and is traditionally associated with the shepherds of the mountains of Lazio and Abruzzo. When they migrated seasonally with their flocks, they carried long-keeping dried pasta, sheep's cheese and black pepper, so they could quickly cook a hot meal in the open. The history of Pecorino Romano goes back to ancient Roman times, and it is still one of the most important cheeses in Roman cuisine.

ranking.name: Bucatini all'amatriciana
ranking.description: A sauce made from cured pork cheek, tomato, Pecorino cheese and chili pepper, traditionally tossed with bucatini or long pasta, tangy, salty and savory.
ranking.history: The dish is named after Amatrice, a small mountain town in Lazio, which until 1927 belonged to the Abruzzo region. The earliest version was the tomato-free "pasta alla gricia," and tomato was added to produce today's form only after it became common in the late 18th century; it was then brought to Rome by Amatrice cooks working there. In 2016 Amatrice was struck by a major earthquake, and restaurants around the world sold this pasta to raise funds for the disaster area, making it a symbol of solidarity and rebuilding.

ranking.name: Saltimbocca
ranking.description: Veal slices are topped with prosciutto and sage leaves, fastened with toothpicks, pan-fried in butter and finished with a white wine reduction; it is savory and juicy.
ranking.history: "Saltimbocca" means "jump into the mouth," describing how delicious it is, so that one cannot help eating bite after bite. In 1891 the Italian food writer Pellegrino Artusi included the Roman version in his classic Science in the Kitchen and the Art of Eating Well, making the dish widely known. It is a classic main course in Roman restaurants and also shows Roman cuisine's skill in using simple ingredients and herbs.

ranking.name: Supplì
ranking.description: Rice cooked in tomato sauce or meat ragù is shaped into an oval with a piece of mozzarella in the center, coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried; when bitten open, the cheese stretches in strings.
ranking.history: The name supplì is generally believed to come from the French "surprise," linked with French influence during the Napoleonic army's occupation of Rome in the early 19th century, referring to the cheese discovered in the middle only after biting in. Because the stretched cheese looks like a telephone cord, Romans also call it "supplì al telefono." It is the most typical street snack at Roman pizzerias and snack shops, and a similar but distinct regional tradition from Sicily's arancini.
